desc:
A queen attacks every square in her row, in her column and on both of her diagonals. You are given the positions of some queens on a very large chessboard as queens, where queens[i] = [row, col]. All positions are different.

Return true if no two queens attack each other, that is, if no two queens share a row, a column or a diagonal. Queens standing in between do not matter: if two queens lie on a common line, the board is unsafe.

queens = [[0,1],[1,3],[2,0],[3,2]]  →  true
queens = [[0,0],[2,1],[1,2]]        →  false   ((2,1) and (1,2) share a diagonal)
hints: Two queens clash when they agree on a row, on a column, or on a diagonal. Comparing all pairs works but costs O(m<sup>2</sup>). Can you detect a clash while scanning once?
Along one diagonal the value row - col never changes. Along the other diagonal the value row + col never changes.
Keep four sets: used rows, used columns, used values of row - col and used values of row + col. If a new queen hits any of them, return false.
editorial: Every line a queen attacks along is described by one number: the row index, the column index, row - col for the diagonals that go down-right, and row + col for the diagonals that go down-left. Two queens attack each other exactly when they share one of these four numbers.

Scan the queens once and keep four hash sets. If a queen's row, column, row - col or row + col is already in its set, the board is unsafe; otherwise insert the four values. This is O(m) time and space, and it is the same bookkeeping that makes N-Queens backtracking fast: a diagonal is just a number you can mark as used.
